# Calibration: when 0.8 really means 80% {#sec-ch03}

::: {.epigraph by="Lord Kelvin, lecture on electrical units of measurement, 1883"}
When you can measure what you are speaking about, and express it in numbers, you know something about it.
:::

*"If a model says 80%, does that mean 80%?"* It sounds silly until it costs you money.

A number is just a number. A model can say 0.8 about alerts that are attacks half the time, or nineteen times in twenty. Nothing in its maths forces its 0.8 to match reality. It matches only if the model was built well and *checked*, and even then it can drift.

This chapter is about checking: the most important habit in the book. Every threshold, policy and claim about Jev later on depends on it.

::: {.goals}
- Say what it means for a model to be *calibrated*, and why that's different from being accurate.
- Read a reliability diagram and the expected calibration error (ECE).
- Recognise the everyday mistakes that break calibration, including rebalancing your training data.
- Fix a miscalibrated model with Platt scaling, temperature scaling or isotonic regression, and know which to use.
- Check calibration within the groups you'll actually act on.
:::

## The weather forecaster's secret

In the 1970s, researchers checked American weather forecasters against what actually happened. When they said "30% chance of rain", it rained on about 30% of those days. When they said 70%, about 70%. Across the whole range, what they said matched what happened almost perfectly [@murphy1977].

Most people are nothing like this. Ask someone for a range they're "90% sure" contains a quiz answer, and the answer falls inside far less than 90% of the time. People are too sure of themselves.

![Two forecasters. For each thing they said ("30%", "70%" and so on), we count how often it actually happened. The careful forecaster sits on the diagonal: their 70% happens about 70% of the time. The overconfident one says 90% about things that happen only about 70% of the time.](/figures/ch04/forecasters.pdf){#fig-forecasters}

Forecasters aren't good because they're always right; they can't be. They're good because their numbers mean what they say. That's **calibration**.

::: {.keyidea}
A model is calibrated when its 80% happens about 80% of the time.
:::

And you can check it with nothing but grouping and counting: collect everything the model called "about 80%", and count how often it happened.

## Good at ranking, badly calibrated

People constantly confuse two different things a model's numbers can be good at.

**Ranking**: do attacks get higher numbers than harmless alerts? Sort by the model's score; do the real attacks rise to the top? The **AUC** measures this: the chance that a random attack scores above a random harmless alert. 1 is perfect; 0.5 is a coin toss.

**Calibration**: when the model says 0.3, are three in ten of those alerts attacks?

A model can rank perfectly and still be badly wrong about how sure it is.

![Two models, identical at ranking (same AUC) but not at calibration. Model A is the logistic regression from Chapter 2. Model B is the same model with its probabilities distorted: it still sorts the alerts in the same order, but its numbers no longer mean anything.](/figures/ch04/same-auc.pdf){#fig-same-auc}

Both models in @fig-same-auc have AUC {{< num ch04 lr.auc f3 >}}. Model B says 40% about alerts that are attacks only a few percent of the time. If you only sort, B is as good as A. The moment you put a threshold on its numbers, or multiply them by a cost, it misleads you.

Here's the trap: leaderboards report ranking scores (AUC, accuracy, F1). Calibration is often not measured at all. For a decision system, it's usually what matters most.

::: {.keyidea}
Ranking well and being calibrated are different skills; decisions need both.
:::

## The reliability diagram

Check the way the weather researchers did:

1. Take predictions where you know what happened (test alerts the model never trained on).
2. Sort them into bins by what the model said: 0–10%, 10–20% and so on.
3. In each bin, compare two numbers: the model's *average* prediction and the share of alerts that really were attacks.
4. Plot one against the other.

That plot is called a **reliability diagram**, and you'll see a lot of them from here on.

![The reliability diagram of our Chapter 2 model on alerts it never saw. Points on the dashed diagonal mean the model's numbers can be trusted as they are. Underneath, a histogram (log scale) shows how many alerts fall in each part of the range: most are near zero, and only a few are above 50%.](/figures/ch04/anatomy.pdf){#fig-anatomy-03}

Read @fig-anatomy-03 top and bottom together; people forget the bottom. Where there's plenty of data, the points sit near the diagonal. At the right end they jump around, and the histogram says why: only a few dozen alerts live there. A dot built on twelve alerts is weak evidence. Look at the counts before you worry, or relax.

### One number: ECE

Sometimes you need one number, to compare models or to set off an alarm when calibration slips. The usual one is the **expected calibration error (ECE)**: the average gap between "said" and "happened" across the bins, weighted by how many predictions each holds [@naeini2015]. Our model's ECE is {{< num ch04 lr.ece f3 >}}: off by under one percentage point on average. Model B's is {{< num ch04 squashed.ece f2 >}}.

ECE is an average, so it can hide a badly calibrated corner, and the high end, where the dangerous alerts live, is exactly that kind of corner. Report ECE, but always look at the picture.

::: {.deeper}
The **Brier score** is the average squared gap between a predicted probability and what happened (1 or 0). Allan Murphy showed that it splits into three parts [@murphy1973]: Brier = *reliability* − *resolution* + *uncertainty*. **Uncertainty** is how hard the problem is to begin with (it depends only on the base rate).

**Resolution** is how well the model's predictions separate cases that turn out differently; it's close to ranking skill. **Reliability** is the calibration error: the squared gap between said and happened, bin by bin. For our model: reliability {{< num ch04 decomposition.reliability f4 >}}, resolution {{< num ch04 decomposition.resolution f4 >}}, uncertainty {{< num ch04 decomposition.uncertainty f4 >}}. A model can improve its Brier score by ranking better or by being better calibrated. The three parts tell you which.
:::

## How calibration breaks

If log loss rewards honesty, why would a model come out miscalibrated? Because training can mislead it. The usual causes:

**Rebalancing the data.** The most common, and usually well meant. Attacks are rare ({{< num ch04 base pct >}}), so someone trains on a 50/50 mix "so the model sees more attacks". The ranking stays fine. But the model has learned a world where attacks are *common*, and it honestly reports probabilities for that world, not ours.

![A model trained on 50/50 rebalanced data (red, solid line with squares) thinks attacks are about ten times more common than they are, and its probabilities sit far below the diagonal. After Platt scaling fitted on a separate calibration set (green, dashed line with circles), the same model is well calibrated again.](/figures/ch04/rebalanced.pdf){#fig-rebalanced}

Its average prediction is {{< num ch04 bal_mean_pred pct >}}; the real rate is {{< num ch04 base pct >}}. Put a threshold on those numbers and the team drowns.

**Overfitting.** Models that memorise push their probabilities towards 0 and 1, and come out overconfident on new data.

**Scores that were never probabilities.** Some models output a "score" that happens to be between 0 and 1 but was never trained with a proper scoring rule. Treat it as a ranking until you've checked it.

**Big modern networks.** Very large neural networks tend to be *overconfident* [@guo2017]. The "confidence" an LLM states in words is something else again (Chapter 6).

**The world changing.** A model calibrated on last month's base rate is wrong the day an attack campaign doubles the number of attacks (Chapter 14).

## Fixing it

Good news: a model that ranks well but is badly calibrated is usually easy to fix. You don't retrain it; you add a small correction on top. Keep back a **calibration set** the model never trained on, learn a simple function that maps its raw numbers to honest ones, and check the result on a *test* set neither has seen. Three common corrections:

![The three corrections, each fitted to the rebalanced model on the calibration set. Platt scaling learns an S-curve that can shift and stretch. Temperature scaling learns one number that only stretches around the middle, and here it barely changes anything. Isotonic regression learns any rising staircase.](/figures/ch04/fixes.pdf){#fig-fixes}

**Platt scaling** fits a tiny logistic regression on top of the model's log-odds. It learns two numbers: a stretch and a shift [@platt1999]. It's the usual first choice.

**Temperature scaling** fits one number, *T*, and divides the log-odds by it [@guo2017]. *T* above 1 softens overconfidence. It's the standard fix for neural networks, and what people usually mean by "calibrating an LLM classifier".

**Isotonic regression** fits any staircase that only goes up [@zadrozny2002]. It fixes almost any shape, but needs more data and can overfit.

On the rebalanced model, the ECE starts at {{< num ch04 balanced.ece f3 >}}. Platt brings it to {{< num ch04 fixes.Platt.ece f3 >}} and isotonic to {{< num ch04 fixes.Isotonic.ece f3 >}}: almost fully fixed. Temperature leaves it at {{< num ch04 fixes.Temperature.ece f3 >}}, no help at all, and the reason is worth knowing. Rebalancing didn't make the model *overconfident*. It *shifted* every prediction up. A temperature can only stretch around the middle; it can't move everything down. Platt has a shift as well as a stretch.

::: {.keyidea}
Temperature fixes overconfidence. It can't fix a wrong base rate.
:::

## Calibrated on average, wrong for one group

One more trap, the one that bites real systems: a model can be well calibrated *overall* and wrong for one group. Take a version of our model that can't tell which system raised the alert: email, laptops, cloud and so on.

![Calibration checked separately for each alert source. Across all sources together, this model is well calibrated, with an ECE of about half a percentage point. But it overestimates the risk of DLP and Cloud alerts and underestimates EDR alerts, which really are more dangerous here. Averaging hides both mistakes.](/figures/ch04/by-source.pdf){#fig-by-source}

Overall ECE: an excellent {{< num ch04 generic.ece f3 >}}. But for alerts from laptops and servers (EDR), it says {{< num ch04 by_source.EDR.pred pct1 >}} when the truth is {{< num ch04 by_source.EDR.actual pct1 >}}. For data-leak alerts (DLP) it says {{< num ch04 by_source.DLP.pred pct1 >}} when the truth is {{< num ch04 by_source.DLP.actual pct1 >}}. The errors cancel out in the average, and the policy closes too many real laptop attacks.

::: {.keyidea}
Check calibration inside every group you'll treat differently, not just on average.
:::

That means sources, customer tiers, languages, regions, and, when a model affects people's lives, groups of people such as age or gender.

::: {.threshold}
The team auto-closes any alert under 3%. The model above says EDR alerts average {{< num ch04 by_source.EDR.pred pct1 >}} risk, but they're really {{< num ch04 by_source.EDR.actual pct1 >}}. About how much more often than planned will a real EDR threat be auto-closed? Name two ways to fix this: one that changes the model, and one that changes only the policy.

(About 50% more often. You could add the source as a clue, or calibrate separately for each source, so the model is calibrated for every source. Or you could keep the model and set a stricter act threshold for EDR alerts. The first is better; the second is quicker.)
:::

::: {.breaks}
Calibration is always measured *on some data*, and it only holds for data like that. A model calibrated on last quarter's alerts can become less calibrated as tools, attackers and staff change. Isotonic regression fitted on a few hundred examples will overfit and produce rough, overconfident corrections. And calibration says nothing about any *single* prediction: a perfectly calibrated 70% is still wrong three times in ten. Keep a fresh calibration set, refit on a schedule, and keep watching the diagram.
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. Explain to a friend, with no technical words, the difference between a model that ranks well and one that's calibrated. Use the weather.
2. Why must the calibration correction be fitted on separate data, not the training data? What would go wrong?
3. Name three groups in a system you know where calibration might differ, and one decision in each that would go wrong.
:::
